text: In discrete convolution, each new pixel is a {{c1::weighted sum}} of the pixels in its neighbourhood. The weights come from a {{c2::kernel}}, which is also called a mask or a filter.
extra: When the neighbourhood is centred on the pixel, its size has to be odd, like \(3\times 3\) or \(5\times 5\).

text: To convolve at pixel \(P\), you centre the kernel on \(P\), multiply each neighbour by its weight, {{c1::add up}} the products, and write the result into a separate {{c2::output}} image.
extra: Writing back into the input would change pixels that later neighbourhoods still need to read.

text: A smoothing kernel is normalized so its weights add up to {{c1::1}}. That keeps the average {{c2::brightness}} of the image the same.
extra: Smoothing reduces noise, and the price is blurred edges. The scale factor is often written outside the matrix, like \(1/9\).

text: A student writes a \(3\times 3\) mean filter and forgets to divide by 9. On an 8-bit image clipped to 0 to 255, the result is about {{c1::nine times brighter}}, and most pixels end up at {{c2::255}}.
extra: This is study guide practice question 4, answer B. The weights now sum to 9 instead of 1.

text: With the copy border strategy, wherever the kernel would hang off the edge you {{c1::copy}} the input pixel straight to the output. The image keeps its size, but the rim stays {{c2::unprocessed}}.
extra: Know what each border strategy does to the output size and to the border pixels.

text: With truncation of the image, you drop every pixel where the kernel does not fit. The output comes out {{c1::smaller}} than the input.
extra: Copy keeps the size and leaves a raw border. Truncation throws that border away.

text: With truncation of the kernel, edge pixels get a {{c1::modified}} kernel that only covers the neighbours still inside the image.
extra: Corners and each edge need their own cut-down kernel, so the code gets messy.

text: With reflection, a coordinate that falls outside the image is {{c1::mirrored}} back inside it. The lecture calls this the most useful border option.
extra: Circular wrapping treats the image as if it tiled forever, and it is rarely used for images.

text: Unsharp masking first builds an edge image \(g = {{c1::f - S(f)}}\), where \(S(f)\) is a {{c2::blurred}} copy of the original \(f\).
extra: Subtracting the blur removes the smooth parts and leaves only the fine detail.

text: Unsharp masking then adds the edges back with \(f_{UM} = {{c1::f + k \cdot g}}\). Raising \(k\) gives {{c2::stronger}} sharpening.
extra: Typical \(k\) is about 0.2 to 0.7. With \(k\) above 1 it is sometimes called high-boost filtering.

text: A Gaussian filter weights each neighbour by \(w(i,j) = {{c1::e^{-(i^2+j^2)/(2\sigma^2)} }}\). A larger \(\sigma\) gives {{c2::more}} blur, because the weights spread farther from the centre.
extra: The kernel usually reaches out about \(3\sigma\) in each direction. It blurs the same amount in every direction.

text: A median filter replaces each pixel with the {{c1::middle}} value of its neighbourhood after sorting. It removes {{c2::impulse}} noise as long as the bad pixels are less than half the neighbourhood.
extra: It is not a weighted sum, so it is a nonlinear filter.

text: Mean and Gaussian filters reduce noise but {{c1::blur}} edges. A median filter keeps {{c2::sharp edges}} much better.
extra: The downside of the median filter is that it also erases real thin lines that cover less than half the neighbourhood.
